content.title: About
content.content: Blue cheese is a semi‑hard cheese marked by blue or green veins of mold, typically Penicillium roqueforti or Penicillium glaucum. The most famous variety is French Roquefort, aged in limestone caves where natural micro‑flora encourages mold growth. It has a sharp, tangy flavor and a creamy yet firm texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Roquefort is named after the French village of Roquefort‑sur‑Soulzon, where it was first produced in the early 18th century.
Traditional aging takes place in cool, humid caves that maintain a stable environment for the mold.
The cheese is “needled” with a metal rod to distribute mold throughout the wheel and speed up maturation.
There are more than 20 types of blue cheese worldwide, including Gorgonzola, Stilton and Danish Blue.
Blue cheese pairs well with fruits, nuts, honey, and is a key ingredient in sauces, salads and pasta dishes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Blue cheese provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium strengthens bones and teeth and plays a role in nerve function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and blood formation.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: The Penicillium mold can promote beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: During long aging, most lactose is broken down, making the cheese more tolerable for mild lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk or whey proteins should avoid blue cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The cheese is salty; those with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Possible pathogens
items.content: Improperly stored cheese can harbor Listeria or Salmonella.

items.title: Mold spores
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic or asthmatic reactions to mold spores.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve blue cheese in thin slices with bread, crackers, pears, apples or nuts. It is used in creamy sauces for pasta, salads, pizza, and as a topping for steaks. Let the cheese sit at room temperature for 20‑30 minutes before serving to release its aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cheese in its original wrapping or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, wrap in wax paper then aluminum foil. It stays good for 4‑6 weeks. Discard if it develops an off‑smell, unusual mold, or a texture that has become overly crumbly.

collards-fresh-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-to.title: Collards, fresh, cooked, fat added, NS

content.title: About
content.content: Collards are leafy vegetables from the Brassicaceae family, commonly used as a green side dish. The product is available fresh and also pre‑cooked with added fat. In the NS database the fat type is listed as not specified (NS).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards are rich in vitamins A, C and K, as well as calcium and iron.
They are traditionally prepared in Southern US and South African cuisines.
Leaves can grow up to 60 cm long and have a mildly bitter flavor.
They are believed to support liver detoxification.
Fresh collards are often used in salads, while cooked collards appear in soups and stews.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Vitamins A and C help combat free radicals and support the immune system.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium contribute to bone strength.

items.title: Cholesterol reduction
items.content: Dietary fiber and plant sterols may help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Fiber promotes regular bowel movements and gut health.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Iron in collards helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cruciferous vegetables.

items.title: Hypothyroidism
items.content: Large amounts of raw cruciferous greens can affect thyroid function due to glucosinolates.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Collards may enhance the effect of anticoagulants because of their high vitamin K content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh leaves can be added to salads, smoothies, or used as a base for green mixes. Cooked collards are suitable for soups, stews, casseroles; they are often finished with a drizzle of oil to improve flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh leaves in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a slight moisture for up to 5 days. Cooked portions should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

cream-puff-eclair-custard-or-cream-fille.title: Cream puff, custard or cream filled, not iced

content.title: About
content.content: A cream puff (also called an éclair when elongated) is a small choux pastry shell filled with custard, pastry cream, or whipped cream. The dough is made from water, butter, flour and eggs, and the filling is usually sweet, though savory versions exist. These puffs are served without icing, highlighting the delicate texture of the pastry and the smoothness of the cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream puffs originated in France in the 17th century; the name "éclair" means "lightning" in French, referring to how quickly they are eaten.
The classic filling is pastry cream (crème pâtissière), made from milk, egg yolks, sugar and starch.
In the United States the same pastry is often called a "cream puff" and is sometimes served with chocolate sauce, but the original un‑glazed version is considered more authentic.
The dough, called choux pastry, puffs up in the oven creating a hollow cavity perfect for filling.
In Italy a similar treat is known as "bigné" and is frequently filled with fruit or nut creams.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Eggs and milk in the dough provide a modest amount of complete protein, essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy ingredients supply calcium, which supports bone health, and vitamin D when fortified.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The carbohydrate content offers a fast source of energy, useful for a light snack.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and milk contain B2, B12 and folate, which aid metabolic processes.

items.title: Dietary fiber (optional)
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used in the choux pastry, the puff can provide a small amount of dietary fiber.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The cream filling often contains a lot of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Butter in the dough and cream filling add saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Allergy to dairy and eggs
items.content: Cream puffs can trigger allergic reactions in people with milk or egg intolerance.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One puff can contain 150–250 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The pastry is made with wheat flour, making it unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cream puffs at room temperature. They can be enjoyed plain or paired with fresh berries, fruit coulis, or a light dusting of powdered sugar. Cutting them in half allows extra filling such as additional cream, ice cream, or a drizzle of chocolate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cream puffs in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. To restore crispness, gently re‑heat in a 150 °C oven for 5–7 minutes before serving. They freeze well for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge and warm briefly before eating.

nutritional-powder-mix-protein-soy-based.title: NFS Soy Protein Nutritional Powder Mix

content.title: About
content.content: NFS Soy Protein Nutritional Powder Mix is a dry blend containing soy protein, vitamins, and minerals. It is designed to supplement the diet with high‑quality protein and essential nutrients, especially for active individuals or those with limited time for meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy protein is one of the most complete plant sources of all essential amino acids.
The NFS blend provides a balanced macro profile: 20 g protein, 3 g fat, and 2 g carbohydrates per serving.
The mix is fortified with B‑vitamins, vitamin D, and calcium to support metabolism and bone health.
The product is free from gluten, lactose, and artificial sweeteners.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and features a convenient scoop.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: The high soy protein content promotes muscle protein synthesis after workouts.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Soy isoflavones can help reduce LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Strengthens bones
items.content: Added calcium and vitamin D support bone mineralization.

items.title: Provides energy
items.content: B‑vitamins aid in converting food into usable energy, reducing fatigue.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and zinc contribute to normal immune system function.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from mild to severe.

items.title: High phytoestrogen content
items.content: Large amounts of soy isoflavones can affect hormonal balance; stick to the recommended serving size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Some versions contain added sodium; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one scoop (≈30 g) of powder with 250‑300 ml of water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage. It can also be blended into smoothies, oatmeal, or yogurt for extra protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. After opening, use within 3‑4 months for best quality.
